title: The shadow-size studio
subtitle: Spring 2 • Week 4 • Make the same card look larger
objective: Describe how moving an opaque card changes its shadow size when the source and screen stay fixed.

sow.exactOutcome: Explore how the size of a shadow changes; record findings.
sow.alignment: Direct match to the named outcome. The lesson is a 40-minute exemplar, with optional greater depth; no accreditation completion is claimed.

priorLearning: Everyday objects can be described by what we observe.
Use a labelled diagram or evidence card to explain a choice.
success: Name the changed distance and what stays fixed.
Use data to describe the shadow-size pattern.
Predict a suitable card position for a stated target.

vocabulary.meaning: The top-to-bottom size of the shadow.
A simplified account used to explain or predict.

equipment: Small low-power LED source; white screen; rigid opaque card 4 cm high; ruler or tape; stands; printed model data.
preparation: Fix source and screen 100 cm apart. Mark card positions 20, 40 and 50 cm from the source.
Keep card and screen upright and parallel, with source aimed at card centre. Use a small LED to reduce blurred edges.
Pre-check space and visibility. Exact model numbers are not expected from every real torch.
safety: Use a cool low-power LED below face height. No lasers, hot lamps or sunlight.
Secure the screen and stands; keep floor paths clear and lit.
Do not move the light source or screen during comparisons; an adult checks the setup.
practicalAlternative: Use the constructed ideal-model data and diagrams. They describe a point-like source; real measurements can differ because source size and measurement edges matter.

misconceptions.claim: The card grows when the shadow grows.
misconceptions.correction: The same card is used; its position changes how much of the spreading light is blocked.
misconceptions.check: Ask which object was physically changed.

misconceptions.claim: Nearer always means a smaller shadow.
misconceptions.correction: With source and screen fixed, moving the card nearer the source makes a larger shadow in this setup.

misconceptions.claim: Every torch must give the exact model numbers.
misconceptions.correction: The ideal model simplifies source size and sharp edges; real observations can differ.
misconceptions.check: Compare sample model data with an actual measurement label.

access.supported: Choose one route: short choices, word bank and pointing or adult-scribed explanation; keep the same science goal.
access.standard: Use the evidence provided to record a decision and explain the science in short sentences.
access.stretch: Apply the same core idea to a changed setup, identify a limitation and justify a better decision.
access.regulation: Preview the sequence and equipment. Offer seated observation, a quiet paper route, partner rehearsal and a pass. Never require public performance or a darkened room.

sources.title: Department for Education: science programmes of study
sources.note: Checked 8 September 2026. Year 3 light outcomes anchor the BUILD content; ray explanations are carefully modelled as an accessible extension.

slides.title: Same card. Two very different shadows.
body: The card stays 4 cm high.
The source and screen stay still.
Can its shadow change size?
slides.notes: Invite a prediction. State the studio brief: choose a card position to make a shadow about 10 cm high. No artistic drawing ability is required.

slides.title: Keep the shadow idea clear
body: 1. What does an opaque card do?
2. Where is the shadow seen?
3. Is the shadow a solid object?
slides.notes: Answers: blocks light transmission; on the screen; no, it is a region receiving less light. If needed trace the source-card-screen relationship.

slides.title: I move the card near the source
body: The source and screen stay fixed.
The card is 20 cm from the source.
The same card blocks a wider spread.
slides.notes: Think aloud: “I keep the source and screen fixed. I only move the card. I trace the edge rays to the screen: their gap is wide. The shadow is large even though the card has not grown.” This diagram is an ideal small-source model.

visual.title: Change the card position
visual.description: Side-view light-ray model. Ray arrows point away from a small source. Boundary rays pass the top and bottom edges of an opaque card and locate the shadow on a screen.

elements.text: Card is 20 cm from the source.
Fixed source and screen: 100 cm apart

slides.title: I move it towards the screen
body: Now the card is 50 cm from the source.
Its size is unchanged.
The shadow on the screen is smaller.
slides.notes: Think aloud: “I check the same 4 cm card is used. Its edge rays now reach closer together on the fixed screen. In this setup, farther from the source means a smaller shadow.” Do not generalise without stating what is fixed.

visual.title: Change the card position
visual.description: Side-view light-ray model. Ray arrows point away from a small source. Boundary rays pass the top and bottom edges of an opaque card and locate the shadow on a screen.

elements.text: Card is 50 cm from the source.
Fixed source and screen: 100 cm apart

slides.title: I measure the same dimension
body: Measure bottom to top.
Use centimetres each time.
Keep the ruler beside the screen.
slides.notes: Shares I do time. Model zero at the bottom of the shadow, read top at 8 cm. This is a constructed front-view example. Real blurred edges require a consistent chosen edge and a note about uncertainty.

visual.title: Measure one height in centimetres
visual.description: Front-view screen with a rectangular shadow beside a ruler. The shadow runs from zero to eight centimetres; use the same top-to-bottom measure each time.

elements.text: Measure from the bottom edge to the top edge.

slides.title: Find the pattern in the model
body: Compare the three positions.
Which gives the largest shadow?
Use two numbers as evidence.
slides.notes: Every number is constructed ideal-model data, not a measurement made by a class. Pairs place the position cards on a 100 cm line drawn on paper and match the heights. Largest at 20 cm; size falls as source-card distance increases.

table.caption: Constructed ideal point-source model; source → screen = 100 cm

slides.prompt: W1. What changes as the card moves away from the source?
slides.reveal: The model shadow height decreases: 20 cm, 10 cm, then 8 cm.

slides.title: Meet the studio target
body: Target: a shadow 10 cm high.
Choose a card position.
Explain why the other positions miss.
slides.notes: Use the three supplied model cards only. Each pair chooses then tests its choice against the table. 40 cm matches the target; 20 cm gives too large a shadow, 50 cm too small. Real practical pupils should check their measured outcome rather than promise exact equality.
slides.prompt: W2. Which model position meets the target?
slides.reveal: 40 cm from the source gives a 10 cm shadow in this model.

slides.title: Which prediction follows this setup?
body: The source and screen stay fixed.
Move the same card towards the source.
slides.notes: Insist on the stated controls. If pupils say “nearer screen,” make them point to source and screen before restating direction.

options.feedback: The card blocks a wider spread of rays before they reach the fixed screen.
The physical card stays 4 cm high; only its position changes.

options.text: The shadow must stay the same height.
options.feedback: The edge-ray positions at the screen change when the card moves.

slides.title: Choose your investigation route
body: Match the model values.
Recommend a studio position.
Predict between trials.
slides.notes: Give one route only, selected with the pupil. The shared evidence page supports every route. Practical option: test the marked card positions with source and screen fixed. Measure the same top-to-bottom edge convention. Keep actual readings separate from the supplied model. A paper ruler-line and cards give the complete alternative.

slides.title: Use the evidence
body: Read or point to one clue.
Record what it supports.
Keep your explanation short.
slides.notes: Shares the 12-minute independent stage. Practical option: test the marked card positions with source and screen fixed. Measure the same top-to-bottom edge convention. Keep actual readings separate from the supplied model. A paper ruler-line and cards give the complete alternative.

slides.title: Make your own science record
body: Complete your chosen route.
Use a diagram, words or speech.
Check one answer with the evidence.
slides.notes: Allow ten minutes of independent response after the two-minute setup. Practical option: test the marked card positions with source and screen fixed. Measure the same top-to-bottom edge convention. Keep actual readings separate from the supplied model. A paper ruler-line and cards give the complete alternative.

slides.title: Check and improve
body: Does my answer match the evidence?
Have I explained why?
Improve one label or sentence.
slides.notes: Shares the independent stage. Ask the pupil to point to the clue supporting their answer; accept a spoken correction or changed choice.

slides.title: Lundy loop: improve our account
body: Choose how to share one idea.
Listen to another explanation.
Use evidence to improve our account.
slides.notes: Give a private or paired option. Adopt one scientifically sound pupil revision in the class explanation and name the change. No public ranking.
slides.prompt: What must we name when we say “nearer makes it larger”?
slides.reveal: Nearer the source, with the same card and fixed source and screen.

slides.title: Three quick checks
body: E1. What happens to shadow size as this card moves towards the source?
E2. Name one thing kept fixed.
E3. Which model distance gives a 10 cm shadow?
slides.notes: Collect brief individual answers. Secure core requires the main idea and a relevant reason. Revisit the relevant worked diagram next lesson if the explanation reverses cause and effect.
slides.reveal: See the teacher answer guide for the three checks.

pupilPages.title: Evidence: studio model cards
pupilPages.intro: Constructed ideal point-source model. Source and screen stay 100 cm apart. The same 4 cm-high card stays upright.

blocks.text: These numbers are model predictions, not class measurements. Real LED results can differ because the source has size and edges may be blurred.

blocks.prompt: W1. Describe the pattern as source-to-card distance increases.
W2. Choose A, B or C for a 10 cm shadow. Explain.
Observation option: write a real distance and shadow height here. Label it “our measurement”.

pupilPages.title: Route 1 • Match and choose
pupilPages.intro: Use the shared model table. Word bank: larger / smaller / source.

blocks.prompt: S1. Which card position gives the largest model shadow?
S2. Copy the model shadow height at 50 cm.
S3. In this setup, moving towards the source makes the shadow __.
S4. Name two things kept the same.
S5. Which position gives the target 10 cm shadow?

pupilPages.title: Route 2 • Record and recommend
pupilPages.intro: Make a studio instruction from the model evidence.

blocks.prompt: T2. Describe the pattern using two values.
T3. Recommend a position for a 10 cm shadow. State the controls.
T4. Explain why a real torch result might not match exactly.

pupilPages.title: Route 3 • Predict between the trials
pupilPages.intro: The same model now places the card 30 cm from the source. Source and screen remain fixed.

blocks.prompt: X1. Predict whether its shadow is larger or smaller than the 40 cm-position shadow.
X2. Use the table to give two bounds for the predicted height. No formula is needed.
X3. Explain why the card itself has not grown.
X4. A team moves both the card and screen. Can it use our pattern without checking the new setup? Explain.

pupilPages.title: Exit and reflection
pupilPages.intro: Point, draw, write or tell an adult.

blocks.prompt: E1. What happens to shadow size as this card moves towards the source?
E2. Name one thing kept fixed.
E3. Which model distance gives a 10 cm shadow?
R1. Which idea did you improve after hearing evidence?
R2. What would you investigate or ask next?

answers.label: Retrieval 1–3
answers.answer: 1 blocks light transmission. 2 on the screen. 3 no; it is an area receiving less light.

answers.label: We do W1–W2
answers.answer: W1 shadow height falls as source-card distance grows: 20 cm at distance 20, 10 at 40, 8 at 50. W2 40 cm from source; other two produce 20 cm and 8 cm shadows.

answers.label: Hinge
answers.answer: First option correct, with source and screen fixed. The card keeps the same actual height.

answers.label: S1–S5
answers.answer: S1 A, 20 cm from source. S2 8 cm. S3 larger. S4 any two: source position, screen position, card size/orientation, source used. S5 40 cm.

answers.label: T1–T4
answers.answer: T1 20, 10, 8 cm. T2 e.g. moving from 20 to 50 cm reduces model shadow from 20 to 8 cm. T3 card 40 cm from source, same 4 cm card upright and same source/screen 100 cm apart. T4 a real source has size; edges may blur; measurement/positioning can differ.

answers.label: X1–X4
answers.answer: X1 larger than the 40 cm-position shadow. X2 between 10 and 20 cm, exclusive. Optional ideal calculation gives about 13.3 cm but is not required. X3 only position changes. X4 no; source-to-screen distance also affects size, so the fixed-screen comparison no longer applies unchanged.

answers.label: Exit E1–E3
answers.answer: E1 larger. E2 source or screen position, or same card height. E3 40 cm from source.

answers.label: Optional practical record
answers.answer: Actual values vary. Label as measured observations and retain any discrepancy from the model; do not overwrite them with the ideal numbers.

answers.label: R1–R2
answers.answer: Responses vary. Credit a science-related revision or relevant next question. A pass or private response is acceptable; preferences have no fixed right answer.

teacherNotes: 40 minutes: opening 2; retrieval 3; I do 7; We do 8; hinge 3; You do 12; review 3; exit 2. Zero-minute slides share the stage time.
BUILD follows the user’s Year 3 science anchor with age-respectful materials for secondary pupils. Routes are adjustable access choices, not fixed groups or diagnoses.
Every core task can run from the printed evidence. Do not present constructed teaching evidence as observations pupils made. A pupil’s spoken reasoning carries the same scientific value as writing.

For teacher understanding only: ideal shadow height = card height × source-screen distance ÷ source-card distance. Here 4 × 100 ÷ 20 = 20 cm; ÷ 40 = 10 cm; ÷ 50 = 8 cm. Core pupils do not need this formula.
Use the phrase “in this setup”. Distance claims are ambiguous unless the fixed source and screen and the moving card are named.

HTML We do: pupils choose a prediction, test it against the user-controlled SVG model or supplied evidence, then explain or revise. The shared paper cases and W1/W2 prompts provide the equivalent classroom discussion without a device. Any animation is a teaching model, not filmed experimental evidence.
